title: Calibrate an uncertainty-aware Polygraphia III search beyond suffix grouping
statement: A fixed two-sweep unknown-column decoder with an external letter-frequency penalty and a soft inferred-stem exclusivity penalty avoids the earlier 3–7-letter output collapse, but does not reliably recover plaintext. Across five Latin texts and three row-selection seeds, mean held-out character accuracy is .293/.154 for 10 random/cyclic columns, .304/.170 for 24, and .141/.131 for 131. The constrained output uses about 20–22 letters and has much lower unigram KL divergence than the unconstrained suffix model. Cyclic-column iid controls still trigger global-shuffle tests, while known-period matched shuffles mostly suppress that artifact; non-semantic Markov controls continue to trigger the matched test.
check: Develop a probabilistic or otherwise uncertainty-aware decoder for alternative stem/column partitions and context-sensitive homophone collisions. Freeze fitting and search budgets, plaintext-frequency constraints and nulls on independent calibration texts; test on new disjoint books, new keys and longer ciphertext. Compare against a known-column oracle and the deterministic models here, report per-book rather than treating keys as independent texts, and calibrate periodicity inference as well as oracle-period tests. Require genuine planted-key recovery before using the search to rule out a language/cipher cell.
method: Use the pinned Hermes P.III table and five Latin books under the P-J-023 control pipeline. For each target book the external Latin unigram and add-one bigram reference excludes that whole book. Take its first 12,000 plaintext letters for cipher training and next 4,000 for held-out evaluation. For 10, 24, or 131 sampled rows, use three seeds and either independent random selection or a fixed cycle. Generate a real-text, reference-unigram iid, and reference-bigram Markov plaintext per setting, with the same seeded row-selection process. The decoder sees ciphertext word strings and the candidate alphabet, not plaintext, true row IDs, or row table. Four compared methods are frequency-ranked two-character suffix mapping; unconstrained two-sweep suffix bigram search from P-J-023; suffix search with a soft 3×N KL penalty toward the external reference letter distribution; and a word-specific search initialized from that suffix model. For the latter, infer each word’s longest prefix of at least two characters shared by at least four distinct training word forms; otherwise use a singleton group. Penalize by 12 objective units each pair of distinct word forms in the same inferred group assigned the same plaintext letter, plus the same 3×N KL penalty. All searches perform exactly two deterministic coordinate-ascent sweeps with one start. Unknown held-out words use the constrained suffix mapping, then the commonest reference letter. Parameters and budget were fixed for this pilot, not independently preregistered.
null_and_uncertainty: For each held-out decoded stream, compare its bigram loss with 19 global shuffles and 19 shuffles within index modulo the planted column count; add-one lower-tail p=.05 is the minimum attainable. The latter control is given the actual period for cyclic cases, although that information is not given to the decoder, and is merely an artificial stratification for random selection. The evaluator alone reports the training token-weighted majority true-column share for inferred groups, the fraction of training tokens with multiple nested eligible prefixes, and an optimistic held-out type-map accuracy ceiling obtained by assigning each observed spelling its most common true letter. These diagnostics use the planted key after fitting and are not a posterior distribution over columns.
sensitivity: After the initial pilot, repeat the real-plaintext cases at seed 41 using prefix-support minima 3, 4 and 5; report all 90 cases separately. This is an exploratory grouping sensitivity, not an independent holdout or parameter selection for a final claim.
validation: Every one of the 270 main cases asserts that both constrained objectives do not decrease from initialization. All observed character accuracies are at or below the evaluator’s optimistic deterministic-spelling ceiling. Input table and corpus hashes are checked by the imported P-J-023 script.
source: Jürgen Hermes, Polygraphia III: The cipher that pretends to be an artificial language, https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-3313/paper7.pdf; table https://github.com/hermesj/R_Voynich_Stats/blob/0ef1439fa9d90aeab42951a51d0d5a0e27db1f8f/R%20code/Historical_ciphers/keys/ciphers_poly_III_in_order.csv

reproduce.instructions: Save scripts as /tmp/voy_pj024_constrained.py and /tmp/voy_piii_unknown.py and the pinned table as /tmp/voy-piii.csv. Fetch pinned corpora, then run PYTHONPATH=. python3 /tmp/voy_pj024_constrained.py. The sensitivity cases call one(book,n,mode,41,"real") after setting STEM_SUPPORT to each of 3, 4 and 5.

limitations: The penalty encourages but does not exactly enforce the reference distribution. Inferred longest-prefix groups are a deterministic heuristic, not a posterior over column assignments, and multiple nested eligible prefixes are common. The upper bound uses ground truth on test tokens and is not an attainable unsupervised estimate. Different books share language, edition conventions and in two cases a Bible translation; each book’s same test passage is reused across keys, so the 15 cases per cell are not 15 independent books. The iid and Markov generators are limited diagnostics, and 19 permutations have low resolution. A known period is an oracle in the cyclic null, while an unknown period can reduce power. The vocabulary, sample lengths and λ/penalty choices constrain only this search; low accuracy does not rule out richer searches or the broader cipher family. No Voynich or secret held-out manuscript text is used.
